units.translation: The pin, which when it broke it was fated for him to be captured. That it was fated for him to die, Sophocles also says in Daedalus (fr. 161 Pearson).
1659. βελέων: of the rocks; for Homer (Od. 9.495) called the rock thrown by the Cyclops a βέλος. And they say every missile is a βέλος.
1661. ἀνωΐστως: suddenly.
1667a. 〈ἠέρα:〉 darkness. Sᵐ
b. ἐπὶ ζωοῖσιν ἄγονται: by means of drugs they are brought upon the living. Lᵐ P
1671. 〈πρῖεν:〉 he sawed. Lᵍ
1672. δίκηλα: images, phantoms. Lᵐ (P)
1673. ἄηται: is carried, is moved. Lᵐ (P)

1677. βρίμῃ: with strength. From the syllable βρι the verb βρίθω is formed, whose future is βρίσω and the verbal noun βρίμη. For words ending in μη with a single vowel in the penult are barytone, such as χρήμη, φήμη, κνήμη; but those having another consonant before the μ are oxytone, such as γραμμή.
1679. πετραίῳ στόνυχι: στόνυξ is properly the point of a spear, but by extension anything ending in a sharp point.
1693. Salmōnis or Salmōnion, a headland of Crete.
1695. 〈κατουλάδα:〉 the dark night is called κατουλάς from
τὸ ὀλοόν. And in Sophocles in Nauplius (fr. 433 Pearson) ‘in the dark night’.
1698. μυχάτων: of the innermost. Lᵍ P
1700. ἠείδειν: instead of ἠείδεον.
1707. ἀριήκοος: very attentive. The Melantian rocks are two peaks near Thera so named, having their name from Melas who took possession of the region.
1711. Σποράδων βαιή: a small island, Anaphe, named near Thera.

1712. [νῆσος ἰδεῖν] 〈Ἱππουρίδος ἀντία νήσου〉: the island Hippuris near Thera. Timosthenes also mentions it (fr. 24 E. A. Wagner, Die Erdbeschr. d. T., Diss. Lips. 1888, 68) and Pythaenetus in book 1 of On Aegina (fr. 3 M. IV 487).
1725. ἐπεστοβέεσκον: they reviled with words, they insulted.
1733. 〈ἁζόμενος Μαίης υἱα:〉 he says that Euphemus propitiated Hermes
because he had seen a dream. For this god is in charge of dreams; for they attribute dreams to Hermes.
1734. 〈δαιμονίη βῶλαξ ἐπιμάστιος:〉 the clod of Triton upon his breasts; for he called him a divinity (v. 1597).
1745. 〈νεπόδεσσιν:〉 he owed to his sons. Gᴳ Sᵐ
1748. πεμπάζων: counting, reckoning. Lᵍ (P)

1750–57. Euphemus dwelt in Laconia by the seashore. One of his descendants, Samus, settled Thera, whose descendant was Aristoteles, who led the colony to Cyrene. These things are related by Pindar in the Pythian Odes (IV and V with scholia), and more fully by Theochrestus in book 1 of Libyca (M. II 87) and by Acesander in book 1 of Cyrene (fr. 6 M. IV 286).
